claim: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in murine models and possibly also humans.
source: Invariant natural-killer T ( i NKT) cells play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in murine models and possibly also humans.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established knowledge about iNKT cells in asthma models, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: ACC1 (acetyl-coA-carboxylase 1) is highly expressed by lung iNKT cells from WT mice that were developing asthma.
source: ACC1, which is a key fatty-acid synthesis enzyme, was highly expressed by lung iNKT cells from WT mice that were developing asthma.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, where gene expression was measured in iNKT cells from OVA-induced asthma model mice.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced asthma.
source: Cd4 -Cre:: Acc1 fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced and HDM-induced asthma.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing attenuated AHR and reduced inflammation in these knockout mice as shown in Figure 1D and related supplementary figures.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop HDM-induced asthma.
source: Cd4 -Cre:: Acc1 fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced and HDM-induced asthma.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing attenuated AHR and reduced inflammation in HDM-induced asthma models as shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: iNKT cell-deficient mice that were reconstituted with ACC1-deficient iNKT cells failed to develop asthma, unlike when WT iNKT cells were transferred.
source: Moreover, i NKT cell-deficient mice that were reconstituted with ACC1-deficient i NKT cells failed to develop asthma, unlike when WT i NKT cells were transferred.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 3, demonstrating that ACC1-deficient iNKT cells cannot restore asthma phenotype.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associates with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs).
source: ACC1 deficiency in i NKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted i NKT-cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating reduced FABP expression in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associates with reduced expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ.
source: ACC1 deficiency in i NKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted i NKT-cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B demonstrating reduced PPARγ expression in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associates with increased glycolytic capacity that promoted iNKT-cell death.
source: ACC1 deficiency in i NKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted i NKT-cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H demonstrating increased glycolysis and Figure 4J showing increased cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.

claim: Circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
source: Furthermore, circulating i NKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 and PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from human PBMC samples shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
source: Furthermore, circulating i NKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 and PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from human PBMC samples shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: De novo fatty-acid synthesis prevents iNKT-cell death via an ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis.
source: Thus, de novo fatty-acid synthesis prevents i NKT-cell death via an ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis, which contributes to their homeostasis and their pathogenic roles in allergic asthma.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experiments showing the mechanistic pathway including FABP and PPARγ expression changes, glycolysis alterations, and cell death measurements in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis contributes to iNKT cell homeostasis.
source: Thus, de novo fatty-acid synthesis prevents i NKT-cell death via an ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis, which contributes to their homeostasis and their pathogenic roles in allergic asthma.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced iNKT cell numbers in thymus, spleen, and liver in ACC1-deficient mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis contributes to the pathogenic roles of iNKT cells in allergic asthma.
source: Thus, de novo fatty-acid synthesis prevents i NKT-cell death via an ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis, which contributes to their homeostasis and their pathogenic roles in allergic asthma.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that restoration of this axis with palmitate or pioglitazone restores asthma phenotype in adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 6).

claim: iNKT cells express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice).
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells are a subset of innate T cells that express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about iNKT cell characteristics, supported by citations.

claim: iNKT cells respond to glycolipids presented on the CD1d molecule.
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells are a subset of innate T cells that express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice) and respond to glycolipids presented on the CD1d molecule.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about iNKT cell function, supported by citations.

claim: α-galactosylceramide (α-GalCer) originates from a marine sponge and strongly activates iNKT cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: One such glycolipid is α-galactosylceramide (α-GalCer), which originates from a marine sponge and strongly activates iNKT cells in vitro and in vivo
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allende et al., 2008 and Brossay et al., 1998.

claim: Once activated, iNKT cells secrete a diverse array of cytokines, including interferon (IFN)γ, interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-17A, and IL-10.
source: Once activated, iNKT cells secrete a diverse array of cytokines, including interferon (IFN)γ, interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-17A, and IL-10
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abdollahi-Roodsaz et al., 2008.

claim: iNKT cell-derived cytokines play important roles in the pathogenesis of various immunological diseases, including sepsis, arthritis, tumors, and asthma.
source: These iNKT cell-derived cytokines play important roles in the pathogenesis of various immunological diseases, including sepsis, arthritis, tumors, and asthma
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Osuchowski et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Terabe and Berzofsky, 2018; Kim et al., 2005).

claim: iNKT cells are one of the key effectors that promote allergic asthma in murine models.
source: With regard to the latter, iNKT cells are one of the key effectors that promote allergic asthma in murine models.
evidence: This is supported by citations and subsequent experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: By secreting IL-4, iNKT cells stimulate the differentiation of T-helper (Th)2 cells and their responses.
source: Specifically, by secreting IL-4, iNKT cells stimulate the differentiation of T-helper (Th)2 cells and their responses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akbari et al., 2003 and Manson et al., 2020.

claim: By secreting IL-13, iNKT cells promote the contraction of airway smooth muscle, which is a cardinal feature of asthma.
source: Moreover, by secreting IL-13, iNKT cells promote the contraction of airway smooth muscle, which is a cardinal feature of asthma
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akbari et al., 2003 and Manson et al., 2020.

claim: iNKT cells contribute to the development of asthma by secreting X-C motif chemokine ligand-1, which recruits conventional X-C motif chemokine receptor 1-expressing type-1 dendritic cells into the lungs.
source: In addition, we recently reported that iNKT cells contribute to the development of asthma by secreting X-C motif chemokine ligand-1, which recruits conventional X-C motif chemokine receptor 1-expressing type-1 dendritic cells into the lungs: this then stimulates the Th2 responses that drive asthma
evidence: This is supported by citation to Woo et al., 2018.

claim: OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes.
source: Indeed, OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes and tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: OVA challenge tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression in iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes and tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Glycolysis-enzyme expression remained low in iNKT cells after OVA challenge.
source: However, glycolysis-enzyme expression remained low (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: The significantly upregulated fatty-acid synthesis enzymes in iNKT cells after OVA challenge were Acc1, Fasn, and Oxsm.
source: The significantly upregulated fatty-acid synthesis enzymes were Acc1, Fasn, and Oxsm: Acc1 and Fasn play a particularly key role in de novo fatty-acid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Acc1 and Fasn play a particularly key role in de novo fatty-acid synthesis.
source: The significantly upregulated fatty-acid synthesis enzymes were Acc1, Fasn, and Oxsm: Acc1 and Fasn play a particularly key role in de novo fatty-acid synthesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about these enzymes.

claim: When purified murine iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were activated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28, the iNKT cells expressed much higher levels of Acc1 and Fasn than the other cells.
source: Notably, when purified murine iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were activated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28, the iNKT cells expressed much higher levels of Acc1 and Fasn than the other cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressed higher levels of TCA cycle (Sdh2b and Idh1a) and glycolysis (Hk2 and Pkm2) enzymes than iNKT cells when activated with anti-CD3/CD28.
source: By contrast, the CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressed higher levels of TCA cycle (Sdh2b and Idh1a) and glycolysis (Hk2 and Pkm2) enzymes, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Genes involved in the 'lipid, fatty acid and steroid metabolism' pathway were enriched in iNKT cells compared to CD4+ T cells.
source: This is consistent with the previous gene set enrichment analysis of Oh et al.: when they compared unstimulated murine iNKT and CD4+ T cells to each other, they found that genes involved in the 'lipid, fatty acid and steroid metabolism' pathway were enriched in iNKT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al., 2011 and reanalysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: When the Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl control mice were induced to undergo OVA-mediated asthma, we indeed observed that the loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression reduced total immune-cell numbers in the lung and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: we indeed observed that the loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR (Figure 1D) and the total immune-cell numbers in the lung and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with significantly decreased total lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the BALF in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: These changes associated with significantly decreased total lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the BALF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower eosinophil frequencies in the lung in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: and lower eosinophil frequencies in the lung (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The lung CD8+ T cell and alveolar- and interstitial-macrophage frequencies did not change with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: The lung CD8+ T cell and alveolar- and interstitial-macrophage frequencies did not change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The total lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) did not change significantly with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: Importantly, the total lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) also did not change significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: By contrast, there was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung; this was also associated with a significant increase in PI staining (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The drop in iNKT cells in the lung with loss of ACC1 expression was associated with a significant increase in PI staining.
source: By contrast, there was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung; this was also associated with a significant increase in PI staining (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, where PI staining indicates cell death.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression in conventional lung CD4+ T cells (excluding iNKT cells) associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of the conventional lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) showed that loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression but similar Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression in conventional lung CD4+ T cells (excluding iNKT cells) did not affect Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of the conventional lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) showed that loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression but similar Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: When lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both iNKT cells and the conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression with ACC1 deficiency.
source: Indeed, when the lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both iNKT cells and the conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression but similar Ifng and Il17a expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: When lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both cell types demonstrated similar Ifng and Il17a expression with ACC1 deficiency.
source: Indeed, when the lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both iNKT cells and the conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression but similar Ifng and Il17a expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: All findings from OVA-induced asthma were recapitulated in HDM-induced asthma.
source: Notably, all of these findings were recapitulated when we conducted the same analyses in mice that underwent HDM-induced asthma (Figure 1G–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K.

claim: The inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 induced iNKT-cell death during allergen-induced asthmogenesis.
source: Thus, the inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 induced iNKT-cell death during allergen-induced asthmogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased PI staining and reduced iNKT cell numbers in ACC1-deficient mice.

claim: The inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 reduced their expression of Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 in lung conventional CD4+ T cells.
source: This also reduced their expression of Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 in lung conventional CD4+ T cells: these effects markedly reduced the eosinophilia and AHR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced expression of these genes in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The effects of ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells were independent of the inability of conventional lung CD4+ T cells to express ACC1 in the mice.
source: These effects were independent of the inability of conventional lung CD4+ T cells to express ACC1 in the mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the adoptive transfer experiments showing that transfer of ACC1-deficient iNKT cells alone is sufficient to prevent asthma development.

claim: α-GalCer induces iNKT cell activation-mediated AHR.
source: To test this further, we challenged Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl mice intranasally with α-GalCer, which has been shown previously to induce iNKT cell activation-mediated AHR (Meyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2006.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed less AHR in α-GalCer-induced model than control mice.
source: Consistent with the results from OVA- and HDM-induced asthma models, the Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed the following: less AHR and lung and BALF inflammation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed significantly fewer lymphocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages in the BALF in α-GalCer-induced model.
source: significantly fewer lymphocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages in the BALF
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed less eosinophilia in the BALF and lungs in α-GalCer-induced model.
source: less eosinophilia in the BALF and lungs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed no difference in lung CD4+ and CD8+ T cell frequencies but significantly fewer lung iNKT cells in α-GalCer-induced model.
source: no difference in lung CD4+ and CD8+ T cell frequencies but significantly fewer lung iNKT cells and greater PI staining of these cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed greater PI staining of lung iNKT cells in α-GalCer-induced model.
source: no difference in lung CD4+ and CD8+ T cell frequencies but significantly fewer lung iNKT cells and greater PI staining of these cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells failed to promote α-GalCer-induced AHR.
source: Thus, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells also failed to promote α-GalCer-induced AHR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Transfer of WT iNKT cells restored AHR in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: The WT iNKT cells, but not the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, restored the following features: AHR (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transfer of ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not restore AHR in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: The WT iNKT cells, but not the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, restored the following features: AHR (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mature Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice had fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than Acc1fl/fl mice.
source: Mature Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice had fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than Acc1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cell numbers in the thymus and spleen were not affected by Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl.
source: By contrast, the conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cell numbers in the thymus and spleen were not affected by Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ACC1 deletion did not alter the frequencies of the NKT1, NKT2, and NKT17 subsets in the iNKT cell population at any of the developmental stages.
source: However, the ACC1 deletion did not alter the frequencies of the NKT1, NKT2, and NKT17 subsets in the iNKT cell population at any of the developmental stages, namely, stage S1 (CD24+c-Kit-CD44-), stage S2 (CD24+c-Kit-CD44+), and stage S3 (CD24+c-Kit+CD44+) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ACC1 deficiency appeared to reduce iNKT-cell numbers.
source: Thus, ACC1 deficiency appeared to reduce iNKT-cell numbers.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced iNKT cell numbers in multiple organs.

claim: ACC1-deficient BM cells generated markedly fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than WT BM cells in mixed bone marrow chimera mice.
source: The ACC1-deficient BM cells generated markedly fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than the WT BM cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: ACC1 deficiency induced an intrinsic defect in iNKT-cell thymic development and peripheral homeostasis.
source: This confirmed that ACC1 deficiency induced an intrinsic defect in iNKT-cell thymic development and peripheral homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the mixed bone marrow chimera experiments showing cell-intrinsic effects.

claim: When iNKT cells sorted from the livers of Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl mice underwent TCR ligation with anti-CD3/CD28 in vitro, the ACC1-deficient cells produced less CD69 activation marker and cytokine.
source: Moreover, when iNKT cells sorted from the livers of Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl mice underwent TCR ligation with anti-CD3/CD28 in vitro, the ACC1-deficient cells produced less CD69 activation marker and cytokine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: ACC1 plays a cell-intrinsic role in the regulation of iNKT-cell thymic development, peripheral homeostasis, and activation.
source: Thus, ACC1 plays a cell-intrinsic role in the regulation of iNKT-cell thymic development, peripheral homeostasis, and activation.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments including mixed bone marrow chimeras and in vitro activation assays.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells displayed distinct metabolic reprogramming compared to WT iNKT cells.
source: The ACC1-deficient iNKT cells displayed distinct metabolic reprogramming compared to WT iNKT cells.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome and metabolome analyses shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells exhibited low fatty-acid synthesis but high glycolysis.
source: Specifically, they exhibited low fatty-acid synthesis but high glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome and metabolome analyses shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher extracellular acidification rate (ECAR).
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher levels of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and H.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had lower expression of gluconeogenesis genes.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had similar oxygen consumption rate (OCR) compared to WT iNKT cells.
source: However, their oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was similar (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The transcriptome analysis revealed significantly altered levels of cell death-related genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Furthermore, the transcriptome analysis revealed significantly altered levels of cell death-related genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells are prone to dying and this may correlate positively with glycolysis.
source: These observations suggest that ACC1-deficient iNKT cells are prone to dying and that this may correlate positively with glycolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased cell death and glycolysis in ACC1-deficient cells.

claim: The ECAR and cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells correlated positively.
source: Indeed, the ECAR and cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells correlated positively (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Treatment with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis, decreased cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: Treatment with 2-DG decreased expression of pro-apoptotic genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Treatment with 2-DG increased expression of anti-apoptotic genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The effects of 2-DG on cell death and apoptotic gene expression were not observed in WT iNKT cells.
source: These effects were not observed in WT iNKT cells (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: The high levels of glycolysis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells promote their cell death.
source: Thus, the high levels of glycolysis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells promote their cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data and the effects of glycolysis inhibition on cell death.

claim: Sorted unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells expressed Pparg at significantly lower levels than WT iNKT cells.
source: This showed that sorted unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells expressed Pparg at significantly lower levels than WT iNKT cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: When iNKT cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28, the treatment elevated Pparg expression in both WT and ACC1-deficient cell types but much less in the ACC1-deficient cells.
source: This was also observed when the cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28: the treatment elevated Pparg expression in both cell types but much less in the ACC1-deficient cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PPAR-γ may play a critical role in ACC1-mediated modification of iNKT-cell functions.
source: Thus, PPAR-γ may play a critical role in ACC1-mediated modification of iNKT-cell functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression of Pparg in ACC1-deficient versus WT cells.

claim: PPAR-γ is important for activating genes involved in lipid biosynthesis and the maintenance of metabolic homeostasis.
source: This is consistent with the fact that PPAR-γ is important for activating genes involved in lipid biosynthesis and the maintenance of metabolic homeostasis (Ahmadian et al., 2013; Grygiel-Górniak, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmadian et al., 2013 and Grygiel-Górniak, 2014.
